source.title: Rec-Distill: An Industrial Distillation Pipeline for Large-Scale Recommendation Models
source.authors: Haoran Ding; Wenlin Zhao; Yu-Chen Jiang; Juren Li; Jie Zhu; Xin-Chun Li; Yishujie Zhao; Yi Zhang; Ao Qiao; Jianhui Dong; Cheng Chen; Zi-Yan Gong; Deping Xie; Peng Xu; Zi-Kai Wang; Yuwei Wang; H. Yang; Zhe Chen; Yu-Chao Zheng

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The authors use scaling laws to motivate scaling recommendation teachers, but do not test whether the language-model loss power laws, extrapolations, or compute-optimal allocation claims hold.
record.gate_note: The paper reports recommendation-model AUC changes from scaling teacher parameters, sequence length, and data. These are not held-out language-model cross-entropy measurements or tests of power-law form, so the rows are recorded with versions ["none"]. The student capacity and architecture experiments report distillation transferability, not the claim's loss-versus-scale relationships.
record.test_reason: A recommendation-distillation systems paper. It invokes scaling laws (Kaplan, Chinchilla) to motivate scaling the teacher in parameters, sequence length and data. It reports only point AUC gains for single scale-ups (e.g. 1B→7B) and distillation transferability. It fits no power law, has no held-out loss curve, makes no extrapolation and runs no compute-allocation sweep. The only multi-point student scaling curve (Figure 4) gives no numbers and no functional form. Its results measure its own framework's transfer efficiency, not whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that teacher scaling (up to 24B parameters, 20K sequence length, more data) yields gains that Rec-Distill transfers to lightweight students with peak transferability above 60%. They claim this validates scaling laws' practical applicability in recommendation distillation, but they do not fit any scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: Uses recommendation models and reports AUC gains and distillation transferability; it does not fit held-out language-model cross-entropy scaling laws or make compute-optimal allocation estimates.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported results vary with the scaling dimension and data-scaling condition; the paper also reports different transferability across scenarios and student capacities.

fits_no_version.finding: In industrial recommendation models, single scale-ups raise teacher AUC: +0.30% for dense 1B→7B, +0.19% for sequence 5K→20K, and +0.42%→+0.69% when teacher data is added. Distilled students recover a portion of each gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling recommendation teachers in parameters, sequence length or data improves AUC, and a fraction of the gain transfers to smaller students via distillation.

record.problems: The experiments report recommendation AUC gains rather than loss curves or fitted power laws; uncertainty estimates are not stated for these results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's cross-scenario transferability results, Tables 2–4's student capacity and architecture comparisons, and other distillation ablations were not included because they do not measure the scaling-law quantities in the claim.

untested.parts: No held-out language-model loss and no power-law fit over parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters versus data. Chinchilla is cited only as motivation for adding teacher data.
Depth/width comparisons (Table 4) concern student distillation transferability, not loss at fixed parameter count.
Recommendation models are scaled, but only single-step AUC gains are reported. No power-law form is fitted or checked; Figure 4 gives no numbers or fit.
No downstream-task versus scale or versus loss relationship for language models.
No exponents or fitting choices are examined.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 4 claims distillation preserves the student's 'relative scaling trend', but the text gives no values or fitted form, so it cannot bear on V5. No uncertainty is reported for the AUC deltas. All rows correctly carry versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model loss measurements or power-law fits for parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run language-model losses.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token growth trends.
Student architecture comparisons report transferability, not held-out language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
The paper reports scaling gains in recommendation models but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in another modality or training regime.
No downstream language-model task performance or relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss is tested.
No language-model scaling exponents, fit choices, or departures from a single power law are examined.
